sections.heading: Strongly-typed CSS utility classes using C# (supports Blazor, Razor Pages and MVC)
sections.text: FluentCss lets you compose Tailwind-inspired utility classes with a type-safe, chainable API. You write C#, the library generates the class names and the CSS. Get started Browse utilities Generated entirely from C#
sections.code: Generated entirely from C#

sections.heading: Type-safe
sections.text: Every utility is a method. Rename, refactor and navigate styles with the same tooling you already use for C#.

sections.heading: States and responsive
sections.text: Compose hover, focus and active states, then layer responsive min/md and max/md variants on top.

sections.heading: Dark mode built in
sections.text: Use the Dark builder for theme-aware styles, or Theme() for any custom theme name.

sections.heading: Automatic CSS
sections.text: Classes are deduplicated in a registry that emits the final CSS for you.

sections.heading: Installation
sections.text: Pick the package for your hosting model, wire FluentCss up once and start composing styles.

sections.heading: Choose a package
sections.text: There is one integration package per hosting model. Install the one that matches your app. Package Hosting model What it gives you Blazor The component and the preflight stylesheet. Use it for Blazor static SSR, Blazor Server, Blazor WebAssembly (standalone) and Blazor Web Apps using the Interactive Server, Interactive WebAssembly or Auto render mode. ASP.NET Core MVC and Razor Pages The tag helper, the stylesheet middleware and the preflight stylesheet. FluentCss.Core is transitive dependency Both integration packages depend on and bring it in automatically.

sections.heading: Blazor
sections.text: Add the Blazor package: For the shortest syntax add the following to your . Importing the static builder means you can start a chain with or directly. Drop the component into your layout. It renders a block with every class registered while the page is built. Keep the loading and error styles as plain CSS The Blazor template's loading indicator and error UI are present in the HTML before the interactive component tree renders, so in a standalone WebAssembly app they can be visible before has emitted its stylesheet. Put those few rules in a separate plain CSS file (for example ) and link it from or . This documentation site does exactly that: the loading and error rules live in . You do not need the form validation or rules unless you use validation.

sections.heading: Interactive rendering
sections.text: is more than a snapshot of the classes seen so far: it subscribes to the class registry and re-renders its block whenever a new class is registered. A component that renders later on the client - a dialog, a tab or anything that only appears after a click - is therefore styled as soon as it renders, with no page reload. For that to work has to live inside the interactive render boundary. In a Blazor Web App that means the layout, or anything else under , rather than the statically rendered head: Registration follows the process Classes are registered in the process that renders the component. A prerender fills the server registry; interactive WebAssembly fills one inside the browser; an interactive server circuit runs in the server process and shares its registry with the prerender. Whichever runtime is active owns a instance and re-emits the stylesheet when that runtime registers new classes. The Interactive Server, Interactive WebAssembly and Auto render modes are all supported.
sections.code: CssStyles <style> CssStyles <Routes> App.razor <!-- App.razor: the render mode decides where interactivity runs --> <Routes @rendermode="InteractiveWebAssembly" /> <!-- MainLayout.razor: CssStyles is part of the interactive tree --> @inherits LayoutComponentBase <FluentCss.Blazor.CssStyles /> <main>@Body</main> CssStyles

sections.heading: MVC and Razor Pages
sections.text: Add the MVC/Razor Pages package: Register the middleware in . It serves the current hash at and the stylesheet at , with gzip and an ETag. Razor Pages apps map their pages instead with ; the middleware and the tag helper are identical for both models. Register the tag helper and the namespaces in (or ): Finally add the tag helper and the preflight stylesheet to your layout. The tag helper renders the stylesheet and a small script that keeps it in sync after client-side DOM changes, such as a partial view loaded over AJAX. No need to add hash or timestamp The tag helper resolves the current hash when the layout renders, but classes can still be registered after that point. The injected script re-reads on load and watches the document for later changes, swapping the stylesheet when it changes.

sections.heading: Any other .NET project
sections.text: Outside of Blazor and MVC/Razor Pages there is no integration package, so add the core library directly: You can then build classes and read the generated CSS from any .NET application. returns the space separated class names for your attribute, while gives you the stylesheet.
sections.code: dotnet add package FluentCss.Core ToString() class ClassRegistry.DefaultRegistry.Css using FluentCss.Core; var classes = FluentCssBuilder.Css .Background(Color.Emerald500) .Color(Color.White) .Px(6) .Py(3) .RoundedMd(); // "bg-emerald-500 text-white px-6 py-3 rounded-md" string classAttr = classes.ToString(); // The complete, deduplicated stylesheet string css = ClassRegistry.DefaultRegistry.Css;

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: FluentCss turns method calls into utility classes, collects them in a registry and emits a single stylesheet.

sections.heading: The pipeline
sections.text: 1. You call a fluent method such as . 2. A is created: a CSS property, a value and a generated class name. 3. The class is added to a . Duplicates are ignored. 4. The registry appends the CSS rule and invalidates its cached output. 5. on the builder returns the class names for your markup.
sections.code: .Background(Color.Red500) UtilityClass ClassRegistry ToString()

sections.heading: A utility class
sections.text: Every call produces one utility. The builder keeps the class names in order, so the string returned by matches the order in which you composed it.
sections.code: ToString() var button = FluentCssBuilder.Css .Background(Color.Blue500) .Color(Color.White) .Px(6) .Py(3) .RoundedMd(); string classes = button.ToString(); // bg-blue-500 text-white px-6 py-3 rounded-md

sections.heading: Class name format
sections.text: A generated class name is assembled from the active variants, in this order: Utility Generated CSS The same information drives the selector. Variant prefixes are escaped with a backslash so the colon can appear inside a CSS class name.
sections.code: [media]:[theme]:[pseudo]:utility bg-red-500 no variant hover:bg-red-600 pseudo state theme-dark:text-white theme (dark mode) min-md:flex media query theme-dark:hover:bg-slate-700 theme and pseudo min-md:theme-dark:focus:opacity-0 media, theme and pseudo .bg-blue-500 { background-color: oklch(0.623 0.214 259.815) } .text-white { color: #fff } .px-6 { padding-inline: 1.5rem } .py-3 { padding-block: 0.75rem } .rounded-md { border-radius: 0.375rem } /* variants are escaped and scoped */ .hover\:bg-blue-600:hover { background-color: oklch(0.546 0.245 262.881) } @media (width > 48rem) { .min-md\:flex { display: flex } } .theme-dark .theme-dark\:text-white { color: #fff }

sections.heading: The registry
sections.text: is a process wide collection. Because a utility is only added once, calling the same method from several components produces a single CSS rule. The registry also exposes the final output:
sections.code: ClassRegistry.DefaultRegistry // Add through the builder (recommended) FluentCssBuilder.Css.Background(Color.Red500); // Read the generated stylesheet string css = ClassRegistry.DefaultRegistry.Css; // UTF-8 bytes, handy for writing a file or streaming byte[] bytes = ClassRegistry.DefaultRegistry.CssUtf8;

sections.heading: Performance
sections.text: FluentCss is designed so the common case is cheap. This page explains where the cost actually lives and the few habits that keep a large app fast.

sections.heading: Where the cost is
sections.text: There are three distinct costs, and they behave very differently: 1. Building the class string. Every time a chain such as is evaluated, the builder creates a per utility, builds each class name, collects them and joins the result. This runs on every render where the expression appears. 2. Adding to the registry. Each utility is looked up in . If it is already known, the call is a dictionary lookup and nothing else happens. 3. Generating the stylesheet. Only a new class appends a rule and invalidates the cached string. Once every class is known, the stylesheet is never rebuilt again. The short version The registry and the generated CSS settle down after warm-up. The only cost that keeps repeating on every render is building the class strings.
sections.code: Css.Px(4).Py(2) UtilityClass ClassRegistry.DefaultRegistry Css

sections.heading: Precompute class strings
sections.text: Define styles once in a field or get-only property and use the resulting string in markup. The builder then runs once per process, and every render becomes a field read. This is the single most valuable habit. It keeps the per-utility object, string and list allocations, plus the registry lookup, out of the render path entirely. This documentation is built the same way: all of the class strings you see here are precomputed once.
sections.code: static public static class Styles { public static string Button { get; } = $"{Css.Px(6).Py(3) .Background(Color.Blue600) .Color(Color.White) .FontBold() .Hover(h => h.Background(Color.Blue700))}"; } // Rendered as many times as you like, the builder only ran once. <button class="@Styles.Button">Save</button>

sections.heading: Select between precomputed variants
sections.text: When a style depends on state, build each variant once and choose between them. Do not rebuild the chain inside the selection.
sections.code: private static readonly string NavLink = $"{Css.Px(3).Py(2).RoundedMd() .Color(Color.Slate600) .Hover(h => h.Background(Color.Slate100))}"; private static readonly string NavLinkActive = $"{Css.Px(3).Py(2).RoundedMd() .FontBold() .Background(Color.Blue100) .Color(Color.Blue700)}"; // Only the selection runs per render. private string ClassFor(string href) => IsActive(href) ? NavLinkActive : NavLink;

sections.heading: Keep builders out of loops
sections.text: A chain written inside an or loop is evaluated for every iteration. When the set of variants is modest, build the strings once (for example into a array) and index into them.
sections.code:
@foreach @for static readonly private static readonly string[] Swatches = [.. Shades.Select(c => $"{Css.H(8).Grow()} {Css.Background(c)}")]; // ... @for (var i = 0; i < Shades.Length; i++) {
}

sections.heading: Keep the set of classes bounded
sections.text: The registry is process wide and never evicts entries. Every distinct class is retained for the life of the process and, the first time it is seen, triggers a full rebuild of the stylesheet. Utilities that accept arbitrary integers ( , , , , ...) can therefore grow memory and CPU without bound when the values come from user input or computed layout. Keep values on a scale Prefer the fixed Tailwind scale over arbitrary values. Treat any utility value derived from user input as a potential memory leak: the class, its CSS rule and its contribution to the stylesheet are never released.
sections.code: P(n) W(n) Z(n) Opacity(n)

sections.heading: What you do not need to worry about
sections.text: • Calling the same utility many times. A repeated is a dictionary lookup. Do not cache or batch registrations by hand. • The one-time startup burst. The first page that introduces many new classes pays for a stylesheet rebuild per new class, but only once per process and only for pages that have not been seen before. • A handful of inline chains outside loops. A few builder calls per component are negligible next to Blazor's own rendering work.
sections.code: Add

sections.heading: Order of magnitude
sections.text: For reference, on a desktop-class CPU registering 500 utilities takes on the order of a few tens of microseconds when the classes are new, and roughly half that when they are already known. Per utility that is well under a microsecond. The numbers only start to matter when a builder runs on every render of every row of a large list, which is exactly what precomputing avoids.

sections.heading: Checklist
sections.text: ✓ Precompute class strings as members. ✓ Choose between precomputed variants instead of rebuilding. ✓ Move builder chains out of and loops. ✓ Keep utility values on a bounded scale.

sections.heading: Styling with utility classes
sections.text: A utility class maps one small piece of CSS. Combine them to build any design without leaving C#.

sections.heading: Compose instead of names
sections.text: A utility does one thing: set a background, a padding, a display mode, and so on. Instead of inventing a class name for every component, you chain a handful of utilities together. Card title A few chained utilities.

sections.heading: Entry points
sections.text: Every chain starts with one of three roots. The root decides the variant prefix applied to the whole chain. Utility Generated CSS
sections.code: Css no prefix, theme-neutral styles Dark theme-dark: prefix, applies inside the dark theme Theme("halloween") theme-halloween: prefix, any custom theme

sections.heading: Chaining
sections.text: Utility methods return the builder, so calls can be chained or spread over several statements. Each call registers a class immediately.
sections.code: // One chain, many utilities var card = FluentCssBuilder.Css .P(6) .RoundedLg() .Background(Color.White) .ShadowMd(); // Or spread over statements; they register in order card = card.Color(Color.Slate900); card = card.Hover(h => h.ShadowLg());

sections.heading: Using the result in Razor
sections.text: On a plain HTML element you can call the builder inline. FluentCss returns an object whose is the class attribute value. Styled inline on an HTML element. Blazor components need a variable Blazor does not allow complex C# expressions in the attributes of a component. The inline chain below will not compile. Precompute the class string and pass a simple variable instead. A common pattern is to keep reusable class strings in a static class. Because the builder works anywhere, the strings can be cached and shared. Inside a component the result can also be interpolated with other expressions:

sections.heading: Deduplication
sections.text: Registering the same utility twice only emits one CSS rule. The registry compares classes by their generated name, so the more often a utility is used the more the stylesheet is reused.
sections.code: var a = new ClassRegistry(); a.Add(new UtilityClass("p-4", "padding", "1rem")); a.Add(new UtilityClass("p-4", "padding", "1rem")); // ignored // a.Css contains exactly one .p-4 rule

sections.heading: Extensibility
sections.text: FluentCss is a small set of primitives. Because utilities are ordinary C# methods and values are typed, you can grow the API with your own tokens and helper methods.

sections.heading: Primitives, not a fixed API
sections.text: The library gives you typed values ( , , , ) and builder methods that accept them. Anything project-specific — a spacing scale, a brand palette, a card helper — belongs in your application, not in the library.
sections.code: Color Length Size FontFamily

sections.heading: Define your own tokens
sections.text: A token is just a named value. Group related values in a static class; the name becomes the class fragment and the value is emitted as-is.
sections.code: Length public static class Spacing { public static readonly Length Xs = new("0.25rem", "1"); // p-1 public static readonly Length Sm = new("0.5rem", "2"); // p-2 public static readonly Length Md = new("1rem", "4"); // p-4 public static readonly Length Lg = new("1.5rem", "6"); // p-6 public static readonly Length Xl = new("2rem", "8"); // p-8 } // The name is the class token, so these reuse the numeric class names // that P(1)..P(8) already produce and deduplicate with them. Css.P(Spacing.Md).Gap(Spacing.Md); // classes: p-4 gap-4

sections.heading: Add helper methods
sections.text: Turn repeated chains into extension methods. A helper is a normal static method whose first parameter is the builder; return the same interface so calls keep chaining. Which interface should I extend? — implemented by every builder. Best for helpers that only set values, and the only choice that also works inside , and . — the normal builder returned by , and . Use it when the helper chains several utilities. — the root only. Required for , and . — the parameter passed to the / / callbacks.
sections.code: public static class StyleExtensions { // IStyleBuilder<T> is implemented by every builder, so this works on // Css, Dark, Theme("...") and inside Hover/Focus/Active. public static T Padded<T>(this IStyleBuilder<T> builder, Length length) => builder.P(length); // A concrete interface can chain and return the same type. public static IFluentCssBuilder SpacingMd(this IFluentCssBuilder builder) => builder.P(Spacing.Md).Gap(Spacing.Md); } // usage Css.Padded(Spacing.Lg); Css.SpacingMd(); IStyleBuilder<T> Hover Focus Active IFluentCssBuilder Css Dark Theme(...) IRootFluentCssBuilder Min Max Media IOnlyStyleBuilder Hover Focus Active

sections.heading: Arbitrary declarations
sections.text: When no typed helper covers a CSS property, use the escape hatch. It emits one utility with a class name, a property and a value. The class name is the identity used for deduplication, so keep it unique and stable. Prefer typed helpers is stringly-typed. Prefer , , , and the built-in methods when they exist; reach for only for the gaps.
sections.code: Arbitrary // Arbitrary("class-name", "css-property", "css-value") Css.Arbitrary("font-350", "font-weight", "350"); Css.Arbitrary("aspect-golden", "aspect-ratio", "1.618 / 1"); Css.Arbitrary("grid-dashboard", "grid-template-columns", "240px 1fr"); // It composes with states and media like any other utility: Css.Hover(h => h.Arbitrary("font-350", "font-weight", "350")); Css.MinMd(md => md.Arbitrary("text-huge", "font-size", "4rem")); Arbitrary Color Length Size FontFamily Arbitrary

sections.heading: Responsive and state helpers
sections.text: Root and callback helpers follow the same idea, targeting the interface that has the methods you need.
sections.code: public static class ResponsiveExtensions { // IRootFluentCssBuilder is required for media and theme helpers. public static IRootFluentCssBuilder StackOnMd(this IRootFluentCssBuilder builder) => builder.MinMd(md => md.Flex(FlexDirection.Row)); // IOnlyStyleBuilder is what Hover/Focus/Active pass to the callback. public static IOnlyStyleBuilder CardHover(this IOnlyStyleBuilder builder) => builder.ShadowLg().Background(Color.Blue50); } // usage Css.Card().StackOnMd(); Css.Hover(h => h.CardHover());

sections.heading: Custom selectors
sections.text: Utility classes cover most styling. When you need a real selector — descendant or child combinators, attributes, :has, :not or a pseudo-element — build it with the typed selector builder and attach declarations with ApplySelector.

sections.heading: Why a selector builder
sections.text: Utilities produce single-class selectors such as . Component styles often need more: , , or . The selector builder lets you write those with typed calls instead of hand-written strings, then registers the declarations through the same registry the utilities use.
sections.code: .p-4 .card > h2 input[type="text"] .card:has(> img) .prose h2::before

sections.heading: ApplySelector
sections.text: The overload takes two lambdas: the first builds the selector, the second declares the styles with — the same builder used by and . A string overload, , is the manual escape hatch: pass any selector text and it is emitted exactly as written, without escaping or validation. Use it for selectors the typed builder does not cover. The and helpers are thin sugar over it. The chain reads in the same order the selector is emitted: media, theme, target, then pseudo. A selector that ends with a combinator such as returns to the target stage, so is .
sections.code: ApplySelector IOnlyStyleBuilder Hover Focus Css.ApplySelector( s => s.Class("btn").Hover(), css => css.Px(4).Py(2).Background(Color.Blue600).Color(Color.White)); // generated .btn:hover { padding-inline: 1rem; padding-block: 0.5rem; ... } ApplySelector(selector, css => ...) ApplyClass ApplyId // Manual selector text, emitted exactly as written. Css.ApplySelector(".card > h2, .card > h3", css => css.Mt(0)); Css.ApplySelector("dialog::backdrop", css => css.Background(Color.Black)); // Sugar: ApplyClass prefixes '.', ApplyId prefixes '#'. Css.ApplyClass("docs-pill", css => css.Px(3).Py(1)); Css.ApplyId("hero", css => css.Py(12)); Child() .prose > h2 s.Class("prose").Child().Element("h2") s => s.Media("(min-width: 48rem)").Dark().Class("card").Hover() // @media (min-width: 48rem) { .dark .card:hover } s => s.Class("prose").Child().Element("h2").Hover() // .prose > h2:hover s => s.Class("a").AdjacentSibling().Class("b") // .a + .b s => s.Class("a").GeneralSibling().Class("b") // .a ~ .b

sections.heading: Compound selectors
sections.text: Classes, ids, attributes and pseudo-classes all belong to the same compound and can be chained in any order. adds the type selector, and adds .

sections.text: builds a comma-separated selector list. Every target shares the surrounding media and theme, and each target is written with the normal fluent chain.

sections.text: , and accept a selector list, just like . accepts relative selectors, so a argument may start with a combinator.

sections.heading: Pseudo-elements
sections.text: A keyword pseudo-element such as ends the selector. Functional pseudo-elements such as return to the compound stage, so a pseudo-class can follow.

sections.heading: A registered component
sections.text: The pill below is a class registered once at startup. Its base rule comes from ; the hover rule is built with the fluent selector builder. Applied rules are emitted before utility rules, so a plain utility class can still override a component style. Registered with ApplySelector
sections.code: ApplyClass // once, at startup Css.ApplyClass("docs-pill", css => css .InlineBlock().Px(3).Py(1).RoundedFull() .TextXs().FontBold() .Background(Color.Blue100).Color(Color.Blue700)); Css.ApplySelector( s => s.Class("docs-pill").Hover(), css => css.Background(Color.Blue200).Color(Color.Blue800)); // usage Registered with ApplySelector

sections.heading: Good to know
sections.text: Applied rules come first Rules registered by are emitted before the utility rules, following component/utility layering. This means a utility class always wins over an applied selector when both have the same specificity. Media sorting A selector that carries its own at-rule ( , , ) is emitted verbatim with the declarations nested inside it. It is not part of the breakpoint sorting that utility media rules get. Startup, not render Register applied selectors once — in a static constructor, a module initializer or your app's startup code. Unlike utilities, applied rules are not deduplicated, so calling on every render would append the same rule repeatedly. One registration per process writes to , which lives in the current process. An interactive WebAssembly app runs your components twice: once on the server while prerendering and again in the browser. Put applied-selector registrations in code that runs on both — a shared static constructor or module initializer — not only in a server-only startup path such as or a hosted service. Utilities are registered as components render, so they are present on both sides automatically; only applied selectors need this.
sections.code: ApplySelector @media @supports @container ApplySelector ApplySelector ClassRegistry.DefaultRegistry Program.cs

sections.heading: Overriding with !important
sections.text: Force a handful of declarations to win the cascade. Important blocks are scoped to a single lambda, compose with states, themes and media, and cannot be nested.

sections.heading: When to use it
sections.text: should be the last resort. Prefer the normal tools first: reorder utilities, add a state or theme variant, or write a component selector with enough specificity. Reach for an important block when you have to beat a style you do not control, such as a vendor stylesheet or an inline style. Hard to override later A rule that uses can only be overridden by another with higher specificity. Keep the blocks small and close to the reason you needed them.
sections.code: !important !important !important

sections.heading: The Important block
sections.text: takes a lambda that receives a styles-only builder. Every declaration added inside the lambda is emitted with , and the returned class names carry a leading . Several declarations can go in one block. Because the is part of the class name, the important utility is a different class from the plain one. Both can live on the page without deduplicating into each other.
sections.code: Important !important ! sections.heading: Composing with states, themes and media
sections.text: An important block is a normal utility chain, so it works anywhere a state, theme or breakpoint callback does. The prefix ends up before the declaration, exactly like any other variant.

sections.heading: One level only
sections.text: The lambda does not receive the full builder: it only exposes the style utilities, not itself. That makes an important block inside another important block a compile error, and stops an accidental flag from cascading through a longer chain. Why not expose Important in the scope? If the scope exposed , the first declaration in the lambda would return the full builder again and the flag could nest. A dedicated keeps override blocks flat. You can still add as many declarations as you need inside one block.

sections.text: For anything outside use and with any value. A is just a CSS value plus an optional name; the factories cover the common units and the constructor handles everything else. Utility Generated CSS To reuse a length, put it in a static class of your own — the same pattern as custom colors. The becomes the class fragment, so a named value gives a readable class ( ) instead of the raw value ( ). The name is the identity FluentCss deduplicates generated CSS by class name. sections.heading: Raw media queries
sections.text: The method is the underlying primitive and accepts any media query and prefix, for queries that are not width comparisons. Modern range syntax The built-in helpers use the modern range syntax, for example . Make sure your target browsers support it, which all current versions of Chrome, Edge, Firefox and Safari do. Priority follows the breakpoint Media rules are emitted in a fixed order, not registration order: min-width helpers are sorted ascending (a larger breakpoint wins over a smaller one) and max-width helpers descending (a smaller range wins). Min rules come after max rules when both match.

sections.heading: How the selector is built
sections.text: A themed utility is scoped by an ancestor that carries the theme class. The generated selector has two parts: the theme scope and the escaped utility class. Theme class goes on an ancestor Because the selector is a descendant combinator, the element that carries must be an ancestor of the styled element. Put it on or a wrapper element, not on the same element that also uses the utilities.
sections.code: /* .theme-dark is the ancestor, the theme class is escaped */ .theme-dark .theme-dark\:bg-slate-800 { background-color: oklch(0.279 0.041 260.031) } .theme-dark .theme-dark\:text-slate-100 { color: oklch(0.968 0.007 247.896) } theme-dark <html> @Dark

sections.heading: Toggling the theme
sections.text: Toggling is plain DOM work: add or remove the theme class. This documentation site persists the choice in a cookie and reads it on the server, so the theme class is part of the rendered element and the page never flashes the light theme first. is kept as a fallback for first visits. This card follows the theme. Use the toggle in the header to switch between light and dark.
sections.code:
localStorage // Read the saved choice. The server reads the same cookie to render the // theme class on , so this only handles the first visit. var theme = readCookie('fluentcss-theme') || localStorage.getItem('fluentcss-theme'); if (theme !== 'dark' && theme !== 'light') { theme = matchMedia('(prefers-color-scheme: dark)').matches ? 'dark' : 'light'; } document.documentElement.classList.toggle('theme-dark', theme === 'dark'); // Toggle it somewhere (for example a button) and persist the choice. function fcToggleTheme() { var dark = document.documentElement.classList.toggle('theme-dark'); document.cookie = 'fluentcss-theme=' + (dark ? 'dark' : 'light') + ';path=/;max-age=31536000;samesite=lax'; }

sections.heading: Applying a theme
sections.text: Theming is plain DOM work. Add the ancestor class to opt in, remove it to opt out. There is no registry call and no re-render: the CSS for the themed utilities already exists and only activates while the ancestor class is present. Why this never leaks to other pages The docs only persist and in the cookie. Custom themes are applied at runtime and are removed by the navigation cleanup in , so another page can never inherit them. If you want a custom theme to survive a reload, store its name in your own cookie and read it the same way the dark theme is read.
sections.code: // Opt in: an ancestor carries the theme class. document.documentElement.classList.add('theme-ocean'); // Opt out again. document.documentElement.classList.remove('theme-ocean'); // Never persisted, so a navigation restores the normal theme. // (Only 'dark' / 'light' are stored in the FluentCss cookie.) dark light docs.js

sections.heading: Border style and color
sections.text: Utility Generated CSS The composite overload combines the three border pieces in a single call:
sections.code: BorderColor(Color.Slate300) border-color: <value> BorderSolid() border-style: solid BorderDashed() border-style: dashed BorderDotted() border-style: dotted Css.Border(2, Color.Slate300, BorderStyle.Dashed); // expands to three utilities: // border-2 border-width: 2px // border-slate-300 border-color: ... // border-dashed border-style: dashed

sections.heading: Custom radius with Length
sections.text: also accepts a , which covers arbitrary values, other units (including percentages) and reusable tokens.
sections.code: Rounded Length Css.Rounded(Length.Px(4)); // rounded-4px Css.Rounded(Length.Percent(50)); // rounded-50% Css.Rounded(new Length("1.25rem", "card")); // rounded-card

sections.heading: Rings and outlines
sections.text: A ring is a based outline that follows the border radius, which makes it ideal for focus states. The outline helpers map to the native property. Utility Generated CSS Focus me Ring
sections.code: box-shadow outline Ring(3, Color.Blue300) box-shadow: 0 0 0 3px <value> Outline(2) outline-width: 2px OutlineHidden() outline: 2px solid transparent <button class="@Css.Px(5).Py(2).RoundedMd().FontBold() @Css.Focus(f => f.Ring(3, Color.Blue300).OutlineHidden())"> Focus me </button>
